en: Cūḷaniddesa:
Exposition of the Pārāyaṇa-vagga 18.
Exposition of the Verses on the Chanting of the Pārāyaṇa Pathway.
"I shall sing the Pārāyana," said the Venerable Piṅgiya,
"just as you have seen, so have you declared."
Vimala, Bhūrimedhasa,
Nikkāma, Nibbāna, and Nāga—
what reason could they have for speaking falsehood?

"They will sing along with the *Pārāyaṇa*; I shall sing along with the song, I shall repeat what has been said, I shall recite what has been recited, I shall speak along with what has been spoken, they will utter what has been uttered—I shall sing along with the *Pārāyaṇa*.
Thus spoke the Venerable Piṅgiya.
“Iccā” is a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhi*)... [and so on] ...this is “iccā” by way of the sequential order of words.
“Āyasmā” is a term of endearment, a term of respect; it is a designation for one who possesses reverence and deference.
"Venerable sir":
*Piṅgiya* is the name, designation, appellation, expression, name, naming, denomination, term, phrasing, and utterance of that elder;
thus, "the venerable Piṅgiya."
“As he saw it, so he spoke”: as he saw it, so he declared, announced, taught, laid down, established, opened up, analyzed, clarified, and revealed.
“All conditioned phenomena are impermanent”—as he saw it, so he declared, announced, taught, laid down, established, opened up, analyzed, clarified, and revealed.
“All conditioned phenomena are suffering” ... [and so on].
"All phenomena are non-self" ...

"Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation"—just as he saw it, so he declared it, proclaimed it, taught it, laid it down, established it, revealed it, analyzed it, made it plain, and disclosed it;
thus, "as he saw it, so he declared it."
"Vimalo bhūrimedhaso" means:
"Vimalo" refers to the stains of lust, the stain of hatred, the stain of delusion, anger, enmity, and so forth,
up to all unwholesome volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), which are stains.
Those stains have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they are cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to the nature of non-arising in the future.
The Buddha is stainless, pure, immaculate, free from stains, having relinquished stains, liberated from stains, and has transcended all stains.
"Bhūri" is said to mean the earth.
The Blessed One is endowed with that wisdom which is equal to the earth, vast, and extensive.
"Medhā" is said to be wisdom (*paññā*).
That which is wisdom, understanding... [and so forth] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.

The Blessed One is endowed with this wisdom, fully endowed, arrived at it, fully arrived at it, possessed of it, fully possessed of it, and equipped with it; therefore he is called the Buddha, the one of excellent wisdom—stainless, of vast wisdom.
He is free from desire, free from craving, and a noble being (nāga).
Regarding sensual pleasures (*kāma*), in brief there are two kinds of sensual pleasure:
sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*).
… [as above] … these are called sensual pleasures as objects. … [as above] …
These are called the defilement-desires (*kilesakāmā*).
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, object-desires (*vatthukāmā*) have been fully understood and defilement-desires have been abandoned.

Because object-desires have been fully understood and defilement-desires have been abandoned, the Blessed One does not desire desires, does not wish for desires, does not long for desires, does not crave desires, and does not yearn for desires.

Those who desire sensual pleasures, who long for sensual pleasures, who wish for sensual pleasures, who crave sensual pleasures, who yearn for sensual pleasures—they are those who desire sensual pleasures, who are possessed by passion, and who perceive through perception.

The Blessed One does not desire sensual pleasures, does not long for sensual pleasures, does not wish for sensual pleasures, does not crave sensual pleasures, and does not yearn for sensual pleasures. Therefore, the Buddha is one without sensual desire, free from sensual desire, one who has abandoned sensual desire, vomited out sensual desire, released sensual desire, relinquished sensual desire, and renounced sensual desire.
One who is free from passion, devoid of passion, whose passion has been cut off, vomited out, transcended, abandoned, and relinquished; one who is hungerless,
extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, and who dwells with a self that has become sublime—
this is called "free from desire" (nikkāma).
"Nibbāna": here, lust is a forest, hatred is a forest, delusion is a forest, anger is a forest, resentment is a forest...
[and so on] ...all unwholesome volitional formations are forests.
These forests have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and are no longer subject to future arising.

Therefore, the Buddha is "without forest" (nibbana), "forestless" (vivana), "devoid of forest" (nibbana), one who has departed from the forest, abandoned the forest, is liberated from the forest, and has transcended all forests— thus he is "without forest.
He is called a "noble one" (nāga).

The Blessed One does not come, thus he is a *nāga*; he does not go, thus he is a *nāga*; he does not arrive, thus he is a *nāga*... [and so on] ...In this way, because the Blessed One does not arrive, he is a *nāga*—a *nāga* free from desire and free from craving.
For what reason would he speak falsely?
"Of what cause" means: for what cause, for what reason, for what purpose, with what source, with what condition—this is "of what cause.
"He speaks falsely" means: he would speak falsely, would tell, would illuminate, would utter.
One who speaks falsely would speak a transgression of falsehood, would speak a lie, would speak an ignoble speech.
Here, someone, having entered an assembly, or a gathering, or the midst of kinsmen, or the midst of a guild, or the midst of a royal court, being summoned and questioned as a witness:
"Come now, good man, say what you know."
Thus, not knowing, he says, “I know”;
or knowing, he says, “I do not know”;
or not seeing, he says, “I see.”
Or, seeing, one says, "I do not see.
Thus, whether for one's own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, one speaks a deliberate lie; this is called the offense of lying.
Furthermore, there are three ways in which false speech occurs.
Before he speaks, the thought occurs to him:
"I will speak falsely"; while speaking, it occurs to him:
"I am speaking falsely"; after having spoken, it occurs to him: [that he has spoken falsely].
“I spoke falsely”—
through these three modes there is false speech.
Furthermore, there is false speech through four modes.
Before he speaks, it occurs to him:
"I will speak falsely"; while speaking, it occurs to him:
"I am speaking falsely"; after having spoken, it occurs to him: [that he has spoken falsely].
“I spoke falsely,” having set aside one’s own view—
in these four ways there is false speech.
Furthermore, in five ways … [and so on].
False speech occurs in six ways, in seven ways, and in eight ways.
Before speaking, he thinks:
"I will speak falsely"; while speaking, he thinks:
"I am speaking falsely"; after having spoken, he thinks: [“I have spoken falsely”].
“I spoke falsely,” having set aside one’s view, having set aside one’s preference, having set aside one’s inclination, having set aside one’s perception, and having set aside one’s disposition—
in these eight ways there is false speech,
a deceptive offense. For what reason would one speak falsely, say something, proclaim it, or utter it?
For what reason would one speak falsely?
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“I shall sing along with the Pārāyana.”
(Thus spoke the venerable Piṅgiya:
"Just as you have seen, so have you declared;
you are stainless, possessed of vast wisdom."
Free from desire, free from craving, a Naga—
on what account would he speak falsely?
For one whose stains and delusion have been abandoned...
Having abandoned conceit and malice—
I shall now proclaim his praise,
a speech adorned with beauty.
"Of one who has abandoned stain and delusion":

here "stain" (mala) refers to the stain of lust, the stain of hatred, the stain of delusion, the stain of conceit, the stain of views, the stain of the defilements (kilesa), the stain of all misconduct, and the stain of all karma leading to existence.
"Delusion" (moha) is the lack of knowledge regarding suffering... [and so on] ...delusion is the fetter of ignorance, the root of unwholesomeness.
This is called delusion (*moha*).

Both stain and delusion have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha is one who has abandoned stain and delusion.
Of one who has abandoned the stain of delusion.
"Abandoning conceit and malice":
conceit is, in its single mode, conceit—
It is the inflation of the mind.
Pride is twofold:
pride consisting in self-exaltation, and...
Pride in disparaging others. Pride is threefold: the pride of thinking "I am superior," [the pride of thinking "I am equal," and the pride of thinking "I am inferior"].
The conceit "I am equal," and the conceit "I am inferior.
Conceit is fourfold.
One gives rise to conceit because of gain;
one gives rise to conceit because of fame;
one gives rise to conceit because of praise.
Through pleasure, one generates conceit.
Conceit is fivefold:
one generates conceit, thinking, "I am a possessor of agreeable forms."
I am a recipient of pleasant sounds …pe… pleasant odors … pleasant tastes …
Regarding tangible objects, one generates conceit.
Conceit is sixfold:
one generates conceit on account of the perfection of the eye.
Through the perfection of the ear …pe… through the perfection of the nose … through the perfection of the tongue …
One generates conceit on account of the perfection of the body... and the perfection of the mind.
There are seven kinds of conceit:
conceit,
overweening conceit, and excessive conceit;
the conceit of "I am superior," the conceit of "I am inferior," and the conceit of "I am."
Wrong pride.
Pride is eightfold:
one generates pride because of gain.
Through lack of gain, one gives rise to self-depreciation;
through fame, one gives rise to pride;
through ill-repute, one gives rise to self-depreciation.
One generates conceit through praise,
generates inferiority-complex through blame,
and generates conceit through pleasure.
Through suffering, one generates self-depreciation.
There are nine kinds of conceit:
the conceit "I am better than one who is better," and so forth.
The conceit "I am superior" toward one who is superior;
the conceit "I am inferior" toward one who is superior;
and the conceit "I am superior" toward one who is equal.
The conceit "I am equal" in one who is equal;
the conceit "I am inferior" in one who is equal;
the conceit "I am superior" in one who is inferior.
The conceit "I am equal to one who is inferior," and the conceit "I am inferior to one who is inferior.
Thus is conceit tenfold.
Here, someone gives rise to conceit on account of birth, or clan, or family lineage, or beauty of complexion,
or wealth, or Vedic study, or field of occupation, or craft, or branch of science,
or learning, or eloquence, or some other such basis.
Whatever such conceit, the act of conceiving, the state of conceiving, loftiness, haughtiness, a banner, grasping, and the desire for self-display in the mind—this is called conceit (*māna*).
As for "sycophancy" (*makkha*): it is sycophancy, the act of sycophancy, the state of being sycophantic, craftiness, and crafty behavior.
This is called flattery.
In the Buddha, the Blessed One, pride and flattery have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha is one who has abandoned pride and flattery.
"Having abandoned conceit and hypocrisy.
Come now, I shall proclaim [them], with speech endowed with praise.
"Come now, I shall" (*handāhaṃ*) is a conjunction of words, a meeting of words, a completion of words, a combination of syllables, a smoothness of phonemes, and a sequence of words.

"Come now, I shall proclaim my speech. "Endowed with beauty" means: I shall proclaim that speech, that utterance, that expression, that enunciation which is possessed of beauty, fully possessed of it, approached by it, fully approached by it, endowed with it, fully endowed with it, and equipped with it.
"I shall teach, I shall prescribe, I shall establish, I shall reveal, I shall analyze,
I shall make plain, I shall declare"— well then, let me proclaim words endowed with beauty.
Thus spoke the elder Piṅgiya.
“For one who has abandoned the stain of delusion,
who has cast off conceit and hypocrisy— listen,
I shall now proclaim his praise.”
"Speech adorned with beauty.
The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the all-seeing,
who has reached the end of the world and transcended all states of existence—
"The Taintless One, who has abandoned all suffering,
whose name is Truth— the Brahmā whom I have served—
is the Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the one with all-seeing vision."
"Dispeller of darkness": he dispelled, drove away, abandoned, removed, eliminated, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent the darkness of lust,
the darkness of hatred, the darkness of delusion, the darkness of conceit, the darkness of views, the darkness of defilements, and the darkness of misconduct—
that which causes blindness, causes ignorance, obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna.
"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One … [as before] … it is a designation based on realization,
namely "Buddha.
"All-seeing eye" refers to the knowledge of omniscience … [as before] …
The Tathāgata is therefore called "the one with the all-seeing eye"—
the Buddha who dispels darkness, the all-seeing one who has reached the end of the world and transcended all states of existence.
"World": one world is the world of existence (bhavaloka). Two worlds: [the world of beings and the world of formations].
The world of existence and the world of origination;
the world of success and the world of the origination of success;
and the world of failure and the world of the origination of failure.
Three worlds:
the three feelings.
Four worlds:
The four nutriments.
The five worlds—
the five aggregates of clinging.
Six worlds:
the six internal sense bases.
Seven worlds:
The seven stations of consciousness.
The eight worlds—
the eight worldly conditions.
Nine worlds—
nine abodes of beings.
Ten worlds—
The ten sense bases.
The twelve worlds—
the twelve sense bases.
The eighteen worlds are the eighteen elements.

"One who has reached the end of the world," said the Blessed One, is one who has gone to the end of the world, attained the end, reached the limit, attained the limit... one who has reached Nibbāna, attained Nibbāna.
Thus, having completed his residence [in the training], having practiced the conduct... for him there is no further becoming in the cycle of birth and death—he has reached the end of the world.
He has transcended all states of existence.
There are two kinds of existence:
existence as kamma and existence as rebirth-linking, which is renewed existence.
What is existence as kamma?
The formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable—
this is kamma-existence.
What is rebirth-existence by way of relinking?
The material form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of rebirth-linking—
this is the renewed existence of rebirth-linking.
The Blessed One has transcended, surpassed, and passed beyond both kamma-existence and the renewed existence of rebirth-linking.
One who has reached the end of the world, transcended all states of existence, is taintless, and has abandoned all suffering. As for "taintless":
there are four taints.

The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance—these taints have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha is one who is without taints.

"All suffering has been abandoned" means: all his suffering connected with rebirth—namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair …pe… the suffering of misfortune due to wrong views—has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, calmed, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge.
Therefore, the Buddha is "one who has abandoned all suffering."
Taintless, having abandoned all suffering— O Brahmā,
I have attended upon him who is called Truth.
"Called Truth" means he is called by the name Truth, called by a similar name, called by a name resembling Truth, or called by a name like Truth.
The Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa—
those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have identical names and identical appellations.
The Blessed One Sakyamuni also has a name and an appellation identical to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Therefore, the Buddha is called by the name "Truth.

"O Brahmā, the Blessed One has been attended by me"— that is, he has been stayed with, attended, waited upon, questioned, and cross-examined— thus, O Brahmā, the one called Truth has been attended by me.
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the all-seeing one,
who has reached the end of the world and transcended all states of existence;”
“The Taintless One, who has abandoned all suffering,
whose name is Truth— the Brahmā whom I have served.
Just as a bird leaves behind a barren field, so did he depart.
One might dwell in a forest that yields much fruit;
even so have I, having abandoned those who see little,
approached the great ocean like a swan.

It says: "Just as one might leave a small grove and dwell in a forest with abundant fruit. A *dija* is called a bird. For what reason is a *dija* called a bird? Because it is born from an egg (*aṇḍaja*). Just as a bird leaves a small grove and dwells in a forest with abundant fruit, so too a wise person leaves a small village and dwells in a large town with abundant alms-food. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born. For what reason is a *dija* called twice-born? Because he is born from a mother and father. Just as a bird is born from an egg and hatches from the shell, thus being twice-born, so too a wise person is born from a mother and father; thus he is twice-born. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again through the higher training in morality, the higher training in concentration, and the higher training in wisdom. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the Brahma-world. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the realm of the Noble Ones. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the state of non-returning. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the state of arahantship. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the unsurpassed security from bondage. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the supreme state of nibbāna. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the noble lineage. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of the Buddhas. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of the Dhamma. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of the Sangha. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of the noble ones. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the fruits. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have entered the path. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have reached the goal. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have abandoned the defilements. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have realized the truths. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained liberation. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the destruction of the taints. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the final knowledge. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the supreme state. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the deathless. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the unconditioned. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the unshakeable. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the island. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the refuge. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the shelter. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the protection. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the sanctuary. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the ultimate goal.

This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the end of suffering. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the cessation of suffering. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the peace. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the bliss. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the coolness. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the liberation. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the final release. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the supreme state of nibbāna. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of the Buddhas, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of the noble ones, the fruits, and the paths. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have abandoned the defilements, realized the truths, and attained liberation and the destruction of the taints. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have attained the final knowledge, the deathless, the unconditioned, the unshakeable, the island, the refuge, the shelter, the protection, the sanctuary, the ultimate goal, the end of suffering, the cessation of suffering, the peace, the bliss, the coolness, and the liberation—the final release and the supreme state of nibbāna. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of the Buddhas, the Dhamma, the Sangha, the noble ones, the fruits, the paths, those who have abandoned the defilements, realized the truths, attained liberation, and attained the destruction of the taints—those who have attained the final knowledge, the deathless, the unconditioned, the unshakeable, the island, the refuge, the shelter, the protection, the sanctuary, the ultimate goal, the end of suffering, the cessation of suffering, the peace, the bliss, the coolness, and the liberation—the final release and the supreme state of nibbāna. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have transcended birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, and have reached the end of suffering. This is the meaning of that. Furthermore, a *dija* is called a twice-born because he is born again in the lineage of those who have crossed over the flood, the bond, the yoke, the attachment, the craving, the clinging, the thirst, the grasping, the fetter, the obstacle, the hindrance, the obstruction, the veil, the covering, the
He is born twice, from the mother’s womb and from the eggshell;
for that reason he is called a “twice-born,” namely, a bird—
a *dija*.
"Just as a bird, having abandoned a small grove— having left it, passed beyond it, transcended it, and gone past it—
might reach, find, and obtain another great forest thicket that has abundant fruit, abundant food, and abundant water."
"And may I make my dwelling in that forest grove"—
just as a bird, having abandoned a small field, might dwell in a forest rich with fruit;
even so, having abandoned those who see little, I have reached the great ocean like a swan.
Thus is the application of the simile.

"Having abandoned those of little vision": this refers to the brahmin Bāvarī and his other teachers—those who, compared to the Buddha, the Blessed One, were of little vision, limited vision, meager vision, inferior vision, base vision, or vision consisting of mere scraps.
Having abandoned those of little vision, limited vision, meager vision, inferior vision, base vision, or vision consisting of mere scraps...
Having abandoned, having transcended, having completely overcome, and having passed beyond the Buddha, the Blessed One— the one of immeasurable vision,
the supreme vision, the best vision, the most excellent vision, the preeminent vision, the highest vision, the most distinguished vision,
the unequaled, the equal of the unequaled, the peerless, the matchless, the incomparable person, the god above gods, the bull among men, the lion among men.
I have approached, found, and attained the Naga among men, the thoroughbred among men, the bull among men, the draft-horse among men,
the bearer of the ten powers. And just as a swan might approach, find, and attain the great Lake Mānasa, or Lake Anotatta, or the great ocean—
an unshakeable mass of water of immeasurable depth— so too [have I attained] the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Unshakable, of immeasurable splendor, possessed of penetrative knowledge, with eyes opened wide, skilled in the analysis of wisdom, having attained the analytical knowledges,
reached the four grounds of self-confidence, pure in resolve, white within, speaking without duality, such-like, true to his word,
non-limited, great, profound, immeasurable, difficult to fathom, abounding in jewels, and like the ocean.
I approached that Teacher, the supreme Conqueror, the Great Sage, who is endowed with the equanimity of the sixfold base, who is incomparable, vast, and immeasurable;
who, speaking thus, proclaims the Path; who is like Meru among mountains, like Garuḷa among birds, like the lion among beasts, and like the ocean among seas.
Thus, having abandoned the small pool, I have reached the great ocean like a swan.
Therefore, the Elder Piṅgiya said:
"Just as a bird, having abandoned a small pond..."
One might dwell in a forest that yields many fruits;
even so, having abandoned those who see little,
I have reached the great ocean like a swan.”
Before Gotama’s teaching, they used to prophesy:
“It was thus,” and “It will be so.”
All that is merely "thus it has been said";
all that is merely an increase of logic—
"those who previously explained it to me."
Yet the brahmin Bāvarī and his other teachers each declared, explained, taught, established, set forth,
disclosed, analyzed, clarified, and revealed their own view, their own preference, their own inclination, their own conviction, their own intention, and their own purpose.
"Those who previously declared:

'In the past, in the teaching of Gotama'— that is, 'in the past, in the teaching of Gotama,' 'beyond the teaching of Gotama,' 'before the teaching of Gotama,' 'earlier than the teaching of Gotama,' the teaching of the Buddha, the teaching of the Conqueror, the teaching of the Tathāgata, the teaching of the Arahant'— this is 'in the past, in the teaching of Gotama.'"
"It was thus," "it will be thus"—thus indeed it was, thus indeed it will be;
this is called "it was thus, it will be thus.
All that is "thus-it-was" (itihītiha), all that "thus-it-was" based on hearsay, tradition, and the handing down of the scriptures.
Whatever they have spoken regarding a doctrine that was not personally realized through direct higher knowledge nor witnessed by themselves, but rather through reasoning, logical grounds,
and reflection on the form of views, and through acceptance based on the contemplation of such views—
all that is "itihītiha" (so they say).

"All that increases reasoning" means all that increases reasoning, increases discursive thought (*vitakka*), increases intention (*saṅkappa*), increases sensual-discursive-thought, increases ill-will-discursive-thought,
increases cruelty-discursive-thought, increases thoughts about relatives, increases thoughts about the country, increases thoughts about immortality,
and increases thoughts associated with lack of sympathy for others.
"Increasing thoughts associated with gain, honor, and renown; increasing thoughts associated with not being treated with contempt—all that is the increase of thought.
Thus spoke the elder Piṅgiya.
“Before this, they prophesied: ‘In the past,
before the teaching of Gotama,’ thus it was, and ‘it will be so.’”
All that is "thus it was said" by tradition;
all that is merely an increase of reasoning.
One who dispels darkness remains alone.
He is possessed of splendor, the maker of light;
Gotama, of vast wisdom,
Gotama, of vast intelligence.
"Solitary, dispeller of darkness, and indifferent. "Solitary":
the Blessed One is solitary by virtue of his renunciation; he is solitary in the sense of being without a second; he is solitary in the sense of the abandoning of craving;

he is solitary as one who is entirely free from lust; he is solitary as one who is entirely free from hatred; he is solitary as one who is entirely free from delusion; he is solitary as one who is entirely free from defilements.
He is "one" because he has gone upon the path traveled by the one; he is "one" because he alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
How is the Blessed One "one" by way of his renunciation?
While still young, with black hair, endowed with the excellence of youth and in the prime of life, the Blessed One [went forth].
Against the wishes of his weeping and lamenting parents with tearful faces, having severed all ties of household life,
having severed the ties of wife and children, having severed the ties of kinsmen, having severed the ties of friends and colleagues,
and having severed the ties of possessions, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and [went forth].
Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness and having attained the state of possessing nothing, he wanders alone, dwells alone, moves about,
conducts himself, protects himself, maintains himself,
and sustains himself. Thus, the Blessed One is "one" by way of his renunciation.
In what sense is the Blessed One “alone” by virtue of being without a second?

Having gone forth in this way, he resorts to solitary dwellings in remote forest thickets and jungle retreats—places that are quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, private from men, and suitable for seclusion.
He goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, and enters a village alone for alms.
He enters [the village], he goes forth alone, he returns alone, he sits in seclusion alone, and he undertakes the walking meditation alone;
he moves, dwells, conducts himself, behaves, protects, maintains, sustains, and lives on alone.
In this way, the Blessed One is "one" in the sense of being without a second.
In what sense is the Blessed One alone in the sense of the abandoning of craving?
Being thus alone, without a second, heedful, ardent, and resolute, as he was exerting himself in the great striving at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River,
he shattered Māra, the dark Namucī, the kinsman of negligence, along with his army, and [cut through] the net of craving.
He abandoned craving that spreads and clings; he dispelled it, brought it to an end, and caused it to cease to exist.
"A person with craving as his companion wanders through the long course of existence."
From this state to another state,
one does not transcend saṃsāra.
Having understood this danger, [one should strive for liberation].
Craving is the origin of suffering;
free from craving and without grasping,
let the mindful bhikkhu wander forth.
Thus, the Blessed One is one in the sense of the abandoning of craving.
How is the Blessed One one as "one who is entirely free from lust"?

He is one because lust has been abandoned; he is one because hatred has been abandoned, thus he is one who is entirely free from hatred; he is one because delusion has been abandoned, thus he is one who is entirely free from delusion; he is one because the defilements have been abandoned, thus he is one who is entirely free from defilement.
In what sense has the Blessed One gone the path that goes in one way?
It is "one" because the path that goes in one way is said to be the four foundations of mindfulness...
[and so on] ...the noble eightfold path.
“The one who sees the end of birth understands the single path, being compassionate for the welfare of others;
by this path, those of old have crossed over.”
"And those who cross over shall cross over the flood.
Thus the Blessed One has gone the path traveled by the one; therefore he is "one.
How is the Blessed One "one" because he has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment? Therefore he is "one."

"Bodhi" is said to be the knowledge in the four paths; it is wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, discernment, insight, and right view.

By means of that knowledge of awakening, the Blessed One awakened to the fact that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and he awakened to the fact that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering."
“He awakened to ‘all phenomena are non-self’ …pe… he awakened to ‘whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation. Or else,
he awakened to that which is to be awakened to, to be fully awakened to, to be awakened to again, to be thoroughly awakened to, and to be realized.”

All that which is to be touched, realized, and fully understood was awakened to, thoroughly awakened to, clearly awakened to, perfectly awakened to, attained, touched, and realized by him through that knowledge of enlightenment.
Thus the Blessed One alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; therefore, he is "alone."
"The Blessed One is the Dispeller of Darkness": he has dispelled, scattered, abandoned, removed, eliminated, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent the darkness of lust, the darkness of hatred,
the darkness of delusion, the darkness of views, the darkness of defilements, and the darkness of misconduct— which causes blindness, causes lack of vision, causes ignorance, obstructs wisdom,
belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna.
"Seated" means the Blessed One was sitting at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya;
he was seated on the side of the mountain.
The disciples, possessors of the threefold knowledge who have abandoned death, attend upon the Sage who has gone beyond suffering.
In this way the Blessed One is seated...

Or else, because all agitation has been stilled, the Blessed One is seated; he has completed his residence [in the training], he has practiced the conduct... there is no further becoming for him, no more wandering in birth and death—in this way too the Blessed One is seated:
thus he alone is the one who sits dispelling the darkness.
"He is radiant, a maker of light.
"Radiant" means he is radiant, possessed of intelligence, wise, endowed with wisdom, possessed of understanding, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.
"Maker of light" means he is a maker of light, a maker of illumination, a maker of radiance, a maker of a lamp, a maker of a torch, a maker of brilliance, and a maker of splendor.

He is possessed of splendor, the maker of light. Gotama of vast wisdom— Gotama of vast wisdom means one whose wisdom is knowledge, whose banner is wisdom, whose ensign is wisdom, who has wisdom as his sovereign, who abounds in investigation,
who abounds in thorough investigation, who abounds in penetration, whose nature is that of one who has penetrated, who dwells in clarity, and whose conduct is directed toward that [clarity].
Abounding in that, making that heavy, leaning toward that, inclining toward that, sloping toward that, intent upon that, and having that as its governing principle.
A banner is the sign of a chariot;
smoke is the sign of fire.
"A king is the mark of a kingdom;
a husband is the mark of a woman.
In the same way, Gotama is one of vast discernment, one whose mark is knowledge, whose banner is wisdom, whose standard is wisdom, who has wisdom as his sovereign, and who abounds in investigation.
Abounding in investigation, abounding in scrutiny, possessing a nature that scrutinizes, dwelling in clarity, practicing that, abounding in that,
making that his burden, inclining toward that, leaning toward that, tending toward that, intent upon that,
and having that as his sovereign domain— Gotama is one of vast wisdom.
"Gotama of vast intelligence": "Vast" (bhūri) refers to the earth.
The Blessed One is endowed with that wisdom which is equal to the earth—vast and extensive.
"Intelligence" (medhā) is a term for wisdom (paññā).
That which is wisdom, understanding... [as above] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.

The Blessed One is endowed with this intelligence, fully endowed, arrived at, fully arrived at, possessed of, fully possessed of, and equipped with it; therefore he is called the Buddha, the one of excellent intelligence—Gotama, the one of vast intelligence.
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“Alone, dispelling darkness, he sits resplendent,
the radiant one who brings forth light.”
“Gotama is of vast wisdom,
Gotama is of vast intelligence”—
he who taught the Dhamma to me.
Visible here and now, timeless,
the destruction of craving, free from calamity—
for which there is no comparison anywhere.
"He who taught the Dhamma to me":

"He" refers to that Blessed One, the Self-Existent, the Teacherless One, who personally awakened to the truths regarding phenomena never heard before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers. "Taught the Dhamma" means...
[he taught the Dhamma].

"Dhamma" means: he has proclaimed, taught, laid down, established, revealed, analyzed, clarified, and made manifest the holy life (brahmacariya) which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing, entirely complete and pure; namely, the four foundations of mindfulness ...
[and so on] ... the noble eightfold path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. Thus it is said.
"He who taught the Dhamma to me"—"visible here and now, timeless":
it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise.
Thus it is "visible here and now."

Alternatively, for one who develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, immediately after that path—immediately following it—one attains, finds, and acquires its fruit; thus it is "visible here and now" (*sanditthika*).
It is "timeless" (*akālika*) because, unlike humans who, having given interest-bearing wealth, do not receive it immediately but must wait for the time [of repayment], this Dhamma is not like that.
One who develops the noble eightfold path in this very life attains, realizes, and acquires its fruit immediately and directly thereafter; it is not elsewhere, nor in another world.
Thus it is "timeless"—meaning it is visible here and now and timeless. It is the destruction of craving, free from affliction.
"Craving" means craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).

"The destruction of craving" means the destruction of craving, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion; the destruction of the course of existence (*gati*), the destruction of rebirth, the destruction of rebirth-linking, the destruction of becoming, the destruction of saṃsāra, the destruction of the round (*vaṭṭa*). "Freedom from calamity":
calamities are said to be the defilements (*kilesa*), the aggregates (*khandha*), and volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
"The abandoning of calamity, the stilling of calamity, the relinquishing of calamity, the subsiding of calamity—the deathless Nibbāna:
this is the destruction of craving, free from calamity.
For there is no likeness for it anywhere."
“Of which” means of Nibbāna.
“There is no simile” means there is no simile, no comparison, no likeness, no counterpart; it does not exist, is not found, and is not obtainable.
“Anywhere” means anywhere, in anything, in any place—whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally.
For whom there is no comparison anywhere.
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“He who taught the Dhamma to me...”
Visible here and now, timeless,
the destruction of craving, free from calamity—
for which there is no comparison anywhere.
Why indeed, Piṅgiya, do you dwell apart from them even for a moment—
those Gotamas of vast wisdom?
"O Gotama of vast wisdom, why indeed do you dwell apart from him? means: "Why indeed do you dwell apart from the Buddha? Why do you go away? Why are you without him?
Why indeed do you dwell apart from him?"
"Even for a moment, O Piṅgiya"— that is, even for a moment, an instant, a brief interval, a lapse, or a duration.
"Piṅgiya" is Bāvari addressing his nephew by name.
"Gotamas of vast wisdom" means: Gotamas of vast wisdom, whose banner is wisdom, whose emblem is wisdom, who are dominated by wisdom;
who are abundant in investigation, abundant in scrutiny, abundant in penetration, whose nature is to penetrate;

who dwell in clarity, whose conduct is that [wisdom], who are devoted to it, who abound in it, who hold it as precious, who are inclined toward it, who tend toward it, who lean toward it, who are intent upon it, and who are dominated by it.
The Gotamas possess vast wisdom;
the Gotamas possess vast intelligence. "Vast" (bhūri) refers to the earth.
The Blessed One is endowed with that wisdom which is equal to the earth—vast and extensive.
"Medhā" is called wisdom (*paññā*).
That which is wisdom, understanding... [as above] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.

The Blessed One is endowed with this *medhā*, wisdom; fully endowed, arrived at, fully arrived at, possessed of, fully possessed of, equipped with it. Therefore, he is the Buddha, the one of excellent *medhā*.
O Gotamas of vast intelligence!
Therefore that brahmin said:
"Why indeed do you dwell apart from him?"
“Even for a moment, O Piṅgiya,
the Gotamas possess vast wisdom;
the Gotamas possess vast intelligence.”
He who taught you the Dhamma—
visible here and now, timeless,
the destruction of craving, free from affliction—
"For whom there is no comparison anywhere.
"He who taught you the Dhamma" refers to that Blessed One...
who had attained omniscience therein and mastery over the powers.

"He taught the Dhamma" means: he declared, taught, laid down, established, disclosed, analyzed, clarified, and revealed the Dhamma—which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—as well as Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna;
thus, "he who taught you the Dhamma.
"Visible here and now, timeless" means: visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise.
Thus it is directly visible.
Or alternatively, for one who develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, immediately after that path, he attains, experiences, and acquires its fruit;
thus also it is directly visible.
"Timeless" means that just as people, having given away wealth that is subject to time, do not receive it immediately but must wait for the right time, this Dhamma is not like that.
One who develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life attains, realizes, and acquires its fruit immediately, right after, and not elsewhere or in another world; thus it is "timeless."
Visible here and now, timeless,
the destruction of craving, free from affliction.
"Craving" refers to craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).

"Exhaustion of craving" means the exhaustion of craving, the exhaustion of lust, the exhaustion of hatred, the exhaustion of delusion; the exhaustion of destiny, the exhaustion of rebirth, the exhaustion of rebirth-linking, the exhaustion of existence, the exhaustion of saṃsāra, the exhaustion of the round. "Freedom from calamity":
calamities are said to be the defilements, the aggregates, and volitional formations.
The abandoning of calamity, the subsiding of calamity, the relinquishing of calamity, the stilling of calamity—the deathless Nibbāna—is what is meant.
"The destruction of craving,
free from affliction— for which there is no comparison anywhere.
"For which" refers to Nibbāna.
“There is no simile” means there is no simile, no comparison, no likeness, no counterpart; it does not exist, is not found, and is not perceived.
“Anywhere” means in some place, in something, in any location—whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally—of which there is no simile anywhere.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“He who taught the Dhamma to you,
Which is visible here and now and timeless;”
The destruction of craving, free from calamity,
for which there is no comparison anywhere—
I do not dwell apart from that.
Even for a moment, O Brāhmaṇa,
the Gotamas possess vast wisdom;
the Gotamas possess vast intelligence.
"I do not dwell apart from him" means: "I do not dwell apart from the Buddha; I do not go away, I do not depart, I am not separate"—thus, "I do not dwell apart from him.
"Even for a moment, O brahmin" means: even for a moment, an instant, a brief duration, a short time, or a long period—thus, "even for a moment."
He addresses his maternal uncle with the respect due to a brahmin.

"The Gotamas of vast wisdom" means: the Gotamas of vast wisdom, possessed of knowledge and discernment, having wisdom as their banner, having wisdom as their emblem, having wisdom as their sovereign, abundant in investigation, abundant in close investigation, abundant in penetration, possessing the nature of penetration, dwelling in clarity, and practicing accordingly.
"Abounding in that, making that their burden, leaning toward that, sloping toward that, tending toward that, intent upon that,
having that as their sovereign"— thus, O Gotamas of vast wisdom,
"O Gotamas of vast intelligence. Here, "vast" (*bhūri*) refers to the earth.
The Blessed One is endowed with that wisdom which is equal to the earth, vast, and extensive.
Wisdom is called *medhā*.
That which is wisdom, understanding... [and so on] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
The Blessed One is endowed with this wisdom and discernment; he is fully endowed, has attained it, has fully attained it, is possessed of it, is fully possessed of it, and is equipped with it.
Therefore, O Gotamas, the Buddha is called "the one of vast wisdom" and "the one of great intelligence."
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“O Brahmin, I do not dwell apart from that even for a moment.”
“O Gotamas of vast wisdom,
O Gotamas of great intelligence!”—
thus he spoke the Dhamma to me.
Visible here and now, timeless,
the destruction of craving, free from calamity—
for which there is no comparison anywhere.

"He who taught me the Dhamma" refers to that Blessed One, the Self-Existent, who was without a teacher; he who, regarding doctrines unheard of before, fully awakened to the Truths by himself and attained omniscience therein, as well as mastery over the powers (*bala*).
"He taught the Dhamma":
"Dhamma" means that which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing, entirely complete and perfect.

He proclaimed, taught, laid down, established, disclosed, analyzed, clarified, and revealed the pure holy life, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, Nibbāna,
and the practice leading to Nibbāna.
"He who taught me the Dhamma...
'visible here and now, timeless'": it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise. Thus it is "visible here and now.

Alternatively, for one who develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, immediately following that path, one attains, experiences, and acquires its fruit. Thus also it is "visible here and now."
"Timeless" means that just as people, having given away wealth that is subject to time, do not receive it immediately but must wait for the time [of its fruition], this Dhamma is not like that.
For one who develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, he attains, realizes, and obtains the fruit of that path immediately, right after; it is not in another time, nor in another world.
Thus it is "timeless"—it is visible and timeless.
"Exhaustion of craving, freedom from enmity.
Craving is craving for forms … pe … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).

The exhaustion of craving is the exhaustion of craving, the exhaustion of lust, the exhaustion of hatred, the exhaustion of delusion; it is the exhaustion of destinies, the exhaustion of rebirths, the exhaustion of rebirth-linking, the exhaustion of existence, the exhaustion of the cycle of wandering, the exhaustion of the round of existence.
"Free from calamity": here "calamities" (īti) refers to the defilements (kilesa), the aggregates (khandha), and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra).
The abandonment of calamity, the subsiding of calamity, the allaying of calamity—the deathless Nibbāna—is "the destruction of craving, free from calamity."
"For whom there is no simile anywhere.
"For whom" means for Nibbāna.
"There is no simile" means there is no comparison, there is no analogy, there is nothing similar, there is no counterpart; it does not exist, it is not found, it is not apprehended.
"Kvaci" means in some place, "kvaci" means somewhere, "katthaci" means anywhere, or internally, or externally, or both internally and externally—
in no place whatsoever is there a simile for him.
Thus the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“He who taught me the Dhamma—
visible here and now, timeless,
the destruction of craving, free from affliction— ”
“For whom there is no likeness anywhere.
O Brahmin, being heedful day and night, I see him with my mind as if with my own eye.
I spend the night paying homage;
therefore, I consider that I am not separated from him.
"I see him with my mind as with my eye"—just as a person with sight might see and observe various forms in the light.
"Just as one might look at, contemplate, and examine [an object], even so do I behold, see, look upon, contemplate, and examine the Buddha, the Blessed One, with the mind"— thus,
"I see him with the mind as if with the eye."
"Day and night, O Brahmin, being heedful": this means that by mentally cultivating recollection of the Buddha both by night and by day, one is heedful—thus, "day and night, O Brahmin, being heedful.
"Worshipping, I pass the night."

"Venerating": whether venerating with the body, or venerating with speech, or venerating with the mind, or venerating by practicing in accordance with what is beneficial, or venerating by practicing in accordance with the Dharma and its sequel;
honoring, respecting, revering, and worshipping him, I spend, pass, and bring to an end each day and night—thus it is said.
"Praising [the Buddha], I pass the night.
It is for that reason that I consider it 'non-separation'; by cultivating that recollection of the Buddha, I consider it non-separation, I consider it not being separated, I know it.
Thus I know, thus I understand, thus I discern, thus I penetrate, thus I pierce through."
For that very reason, I consider it to be non-separation.
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“I see him with my mind as if with my own eye.”
“Day and night, O brahmin, being diligent,
I pass the night paying homage;
therefore, I consider that I am never separated from him.”
Faith, rapture, mind, and mindfulness—
these do not depart from the teaching of Gotama;
in whichever direction the one of vast wisdom goes, [they follow].
"I am led by that very thing:
faith, rapture, mind, and mindfulness.
Regarding "faith": it is the faith directed toward the Blessed One—believing, settling, and full confidence; it is faith, the faculty of faith, and the power of faith.
"Rapture" (*pīti*) means that which, directed toward the Blessed One, is rapture, gladness, rejoicing, exultation, delight, laughter, mirth, happiness, satisfaction, elation, and mental buoyancy.

"Mind" (*mano*) means that which, directed toward the Blessed One, is consciousness, mind, mentation, heart, clarity, the mind-base, the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding element of mind-consciousness.
"Mindfulness" (*sati*) means that which, directed toward the Blessed One, is mindfulness, recollection, and right mindfulness.
"Faith, rapture, mind, and mindfulness—these do not depart from the teaching of Gotama.

These four qualities do not depart, do not go away, do not abandon, and do not leave behind the teaching of Gotama—the teaching of the Buddha, the teaching of the Victor, the teaching of the Tathāgata, the teaching of the Arahant; thus it is said:
"These do not depart from the teaching of Gotama."
"In whatever direction he goes, O one of vast wisdom":
in whatever direction—whether the eastern direction, the western direction, the southern direction, or the northern direction—he goes, moves, proceeds, and advances.
"One of vast wisdom" means one of vast wisdom, great wisdom, sharp wisdom, broad wisdom, laughing wisdom, swift wisdom, and penetrative wisdom.
"Bhūri" means the earth.
The Blessed One is endowed with that vast and extensive wisdom which is equal to the earth;
thus it is said: "Whichever direction the one of vast wisdom goes."
"Because of that, I am bent toward that"—thus he is bent toward the Buddha, inclined toward him, leaning toward him, devoted to him, and dominated by him;
therefore, "I am bent toward that.
For this reason, the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“Faith, rapture, mind, and mindfulness—
these do not depart from the teaching of Gotama;
in whatever direction the one of vast wisdom goes,”
"Because of that very thing, I am now bent over.
For me, who am old and weak in strength,
my body does not move there because of that very thing.
"I go constantly intending [to do so], for my mind, O Brahmin, is yoked to that.
'Of me who am aged, with feeble strength' means: of one who is aged, grown old, advanced in years, having reached the end of his journey, and attained the stage of life."
"Of one with weak strength" means of one who has weak strength, little strength, or limited strength— "of me,
old and of weak strength.
"Therefore the body does not go there" means that the body does not go toward where the Buddha is, does not move, does not proceed, and does not pass beyond.
Therefore, the body does not go there.

"I go constantly by way of intention" means: by way of intending, by way of moving through the range of thought, by way of moving through knowledge, by way of moving through wisdom, and by way of moving through enlightenment, I go, I proceed, I transcend—thus, "I go constantly by way of intention."
“Brahmin, my mind is indeed engaged with that.
“Mind” refers to that which is consciousness, mind, mentation … [as above] … the corresponding element of mind-consciousness.
“Brahmin, my mind is indeed engaged with that” means that the mind is engaged, thoroughly engaged, and fully joined with that by which one is a Buddha.
For my mind, O brahmin, is intent upon that.
Therefore the elder Piṅgiya said:
“Of me who am aged, weak, and lacking strength...”
Therefore the body does not go there;
it is by my intention that I always go,
for my mind, O Brahmin, is joined to that.
Lying in the mud and writhing,
I cried out from island to island;
then I saw the Fully Awakened One.
"Crossed over the flood, free from taints;
lying in the mud, quivering. "Lying in the mud" means:

lying, reclining, dwelling, residing, and living amidst the mud of sensual desire, the mire of sensual desire, the defilement of sensual desire, the snare of sensual desire, the fever of sensual desire, and the hindrance of sensual desire.
"Lying in the mire" means quivering with the quivering of craving and quivering with the quivering of views.
Trembling with the trembling of defilements,
trembling with the trembling of effort,
trembling with the trembling of result.
Trembling with the trembling of mental misconduct,
trembling while impassioned by lust,
trembling while corrupted by hatred,
Deluded, he quivers through delusion;
fettered, he quivers through conceit;
misapprehending, he quivers through views.
One who has fallen into distraction, quivering with restlessness;
one who has entered upon what is undesirable, quivering with doubt;
one who has become firmly rooted, quivering with underlying tendencies.
Trembling because of gain,
trembling because of loss,
trembling because of fame,
Trembling because of gain,
trembling because of praise,
trembling because of blame.
Trembling because of pleasure,
trembling because of pain,
trembling because of birth.
Trembling because of old age,
trembling because of illness,
trembling because of death.
Trembling with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
trembling with the suffering of hell;
trembling with the suffering of the animal realm.
Trembling with the suffering of the realm of hungry ghosts,
with the suffering of human beings...
[and so on] ...with the suffering rooted in descent into the womb.
by the suffering rooted in remaining in the womb;
by the suffering rooted in emerging from the womb;
by the suffering connected with being born; ...
The suffering arising from being born with another’s hostility,
the suffering arising from one’s own exertion,
and the suffering arising from another’s assault.
by the suffering of conditioned formations … by the suffering of change … by the suffering of eye disease …
by the suffering of ear disease … by the suffering of nose disease … by the suffering of tongue disease …
by the suffering of bodily disease … by the suffering of head disease … by the suffering of ear disease …
by the suffering of disease of the mouth...
by the suffering of disease of the teeth...
by the suffering of disease of the lips...
... by coughing ...
by spitting ...
by nasal catarrh ...
… by burning fever … by old age … by a disease of the stomach …
... to fainting ...
to dysentery ...
to colic ...
... by cholera ...
by leprosy ...
by abscesses ...
... by leprosy ...
by consumption ...
by apamāra ...
...daddu...
kaṇḍu... kacchu...
... with maggots ...
with the tearing-away [worms] ...
with the blood-bile ...
... by diabetes mellitus ...
by a carbuncle on the shoulder ... by a boil ...
... for fistula-in-ano ...
for a disease arising from bile ...
for a disease arising from phlegm ...
by a disease arising from wind … by a disease arising from a combination of humors … by a disease arising from a change in the seasons …
by illness arising from the avoidance of uneven ground … by illness resulting from external injury … by illness born of the ripening of kamma …
By cold...
by heat...
by hunger...
for thirst … for urination … for defecation …
by the suffering of contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles;
by the suffering of the death of a mother;
by the suffering of the death of a father; ...
by the suffering of a son’s death … by the suffering of a daughter’s death … by the suffering of the loss of kinsmen …
by the suffering of the misfortune of wealth,
by the suffering of the misfortune of illness,
and by the suffering of the misfortune of virtue...
"Trembling, quivering, shaking, and convulsing because of the suffering of the calamity of views" means:

like one lying in the mud, quivering, they leap from teacher to teacher, from the teaching of the Dhamma to the teaching of the Dhamma, from group to group, from view to view, from practice to practice, and from path to path; they leap, they leap up, they leap all over.
“Lamps lighting a lamp;
then I saw the Fully Enlightened One.
Here, “then” (*atha*) refers to the junction of words, the connection of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of consonants, and the sequential order of words.
"Then indeed.
"I saw" means I saw, I beheld, I perceived, I penetrated.
"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One who is self-become, without a teacher... [and so forth].
The designation based on realization is this: "the Buddha"—
thus I saw the Perfectly Awakened One,
who has crossed the flood and is free from taints.
"Crossed over the flood," said the Blessed One, "crossed over the flood of sensual desire,
crossed over the flood of existence,
crossed over the flood of views."
He has crossed the flood of ignorance;
he has crossed, emerged from, and gone beyond the entire path of saṃsāra, having transcended, fully surmounted, and passed over it.
He has completed his residence [in the training], fulfilled his practice... [and so on] ...the cycle of birth and death.
"There is no further becoming for him"— this refers to one who has crossed the flood.
"Taintless" refers to the four taints.
The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.
These taints have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha is one who is without taints.
He has crossed the flood and is free from taints.
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
"Lying in the mud, writhing about,"
Island seeking an island,
I then beheld the Perfectly Awakened One,
who has crossed the flood and is free from taints.
Just as Vakkali was released through faith,
and so were Bhadrāvudha and Āḷavika Gotama,
even so you too shall release your faith.
"You too, Piṅgiya, shall go to the further shore of the realm of death, just as Vakkali did when he was one whose faith was liberated, and as Bhadrāvudha and Āḷavī-Gotama did.
Just as the Elder Vakkali—faithful, heavy with faith, preceded by faith, intent on faith, and dominated by faith—attained arahantship; so too [shall you].
The Elder Bhaddāvuḍḍha was faithful, one who values faith, one for whom faith is the precursor, one resolved through faith, one dominated by faith,
and one who had attained Arahatship— just as the Elder Āḷavī-Gotama was faithful, one who values faith, one for whom faith is the precursor, one resolved through faith, one dominated by faith,
and one who had attained Arahatship.

"Just as Vakkali, Bhadrāvudha, and Āḷavika Gotama were released from their faith, even so you too shall release your faith—release it, let it go, let it go completely, let it be fully released; have conviction.
'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent'—release your faith, let it go, let it go completely, let it be fully released; have conviction."
“‘All conditioned phenomena are suffering’ … ‘All phenomena are non-self’:

let go of faith, release it, fully release it, be intent upon it, and resolve upon it … ‘Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation’: let go of faith, release it, fully release it, be intent upon it, and resolve upon it.”
In the same way, you too should release your faith.
You shall go, Piṅgiya, to the further shore of the realm of death. By "the realm of death" are meant the defilements, the aggregates, and volitional formations.

The "further shore of the realm of death" is called the deathless Nibbāna—that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.

“You will go, Piṅgiya, to the further shore of the realm of death; you will go to the further shore, you will reach the further shore, you will touch the further shore, you will realize the further shore”—thus, “you will go, Piṅgiya, to the further shore of the realm of death.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“As Vakkali was released in faith,
as were Bhadrāvudha and Āḷavika Gotama,
even so you too shall release your faith.”
"You too shall go, Piṅgiya, to the further shore of the realm of Death.
Having heard these words of the Sage, I have gained even greater confidence.
"The Perfectly Enlightened One has removed the veil [of ignorance];
he is free from harshness and possesses ready eloquence.
In him I place even greater confidence. Thus I place even greater confidence; I have even greater faith; I settle my mind with even greater conviction; I resolve with even greater determination.
“‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’— more and more I am confident, more and more I have faith, more and more I settle my mind, more and more I resolve upon this.
‘All conditioned phenomena are suffering’— more and more I am confident …pe… ‘All phenomena are non-self’— more and more I am confident …pe…”
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation”— thus I become more and more confident, more and more faithful, more and more settled, and more and more resolute;
thus it is that I become more and more confident upon hearing the words of the Sage.
"Silence" (*muna*) is said to be "wisdom" (*ñāṇa*) ... [as before] ... having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage (*muni*).

"Having heard the words of the sage": having heard, grasped, retained, reflected upon, and discerned your speech, your manner of expression, your teaching, and your instruction—thus it is "having heard the words of the sage."
"The Perfectly Enlightened One has removed the veil.
Veil refers to five veils:
the veil of craving, the veil of views, the veil of defilements, the veil of misconduct, and the veil of ignorance.

Those veils of the Buddha, the Blessed One, have been uncovered, shattered, uprooted, abandoned, eradicated, calmed, and tranquillized; they are incapable of arising again, having been burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
Therefore, the Buddha is "one whose veils are removed" (*vivaṭṭacchado*).
"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One... [as before] ...a designation based on realization, namely, "the Buddha."
The Fully Awakened One has removed the covering.
"Ungreedy and eloquent":
here, "greed" means a thicket; hatred is a thicket, delusion is a thicket, anger is a thicket, resentment ... [and so on] ... all unwholesome volitional formations are thickets.
Those obstructions have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they are cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha is free from obstructions.
As for "possessing ready wit," there are three kinds of those possessing ready wit:
There is one who possesses eloquence regarding the scriptures, one who possesses eloquence regarding inquiry, and one who possesses eloquence regarding realization.
What is one who possesses eloquence regarding the scriptures?

Here, a certain person has mastered the word of the Buddha: the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical expositions.
One who gains inspiration by relying on the scriptures is one inspired by the scriptures.
What is one inspired by inquiry?
Here, someone is one who has inquired thoroughly regarding the meaning, the method, the characteristic, the reason, and what is possible and impossible.
Relying on that inquiry, he becomes inspired;
this is one who possesses inspired eloquence through inquiry.
What is one who possesses inspired speech through realization?
Here, someone has realized the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
The four noble paths, the four fruits of asceticism, the four analytical insights, and the six direct knowledges.
His meaning is known, his doctrine is known, his language is known.
When the meaning is known, the meaning flashes forth; when the doctrine is known, the doctrine flashes forth; when the language is known, the language flashes forth.
Among these three types of knowledge, knowledge is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).

The Blessed One is endowed with this analytical knowledge of eloquence; he is fully endowed, has attained it, has fully attained it, is possessed of it, is fully possessed of it, and is equipped with it.
Therefore, the Buddha is "possessed of eloquence" (*paṭibhānavā*).
"For one who has no mastery of the scriptures, no thorough inquiry, and no realization, what could possibly manifest to him?
Thus he is unhesitating and eloquent.
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“Having heard the words of the Sage, I have even greater confidence:
the Sambuddha has pulled away the veil.”
"Wholly wise and possessed of inspired eloquence.
Having directly known the supreme deity,
he understood everything, both high and low.
The Teacher who brings an end to questions for those who profess themselves free from doubt,
having directly known the supreme deities.
There are three kinds of deities:
deities by convention, deities by birth, and deities by purification.
What are the deities by convention?
Conventional deities are said to be kings, princes, and queens.
These are called conventional deities.
Who are the deities by birth?
The gods of rebirth are called the Cātumahārājika gods, the Tāvatiṃsa gods …pe… the Brahmakāyika gods, and those gods who are above them.
These are called the gods of rebirth.
Who are the gods of purification?
The "purified deities" are said to be the Tathāgatas, the disciples of the Tathāgatas, the Arahants whose taints are destroyed, and those who are Paccekabuddhas.
These are called purified deities.

Having known, weighed, scrutinized, analyzed, and made manifest that the Blessed One is the supreme deity among conventional deities, the supreme deity among deities by birth, and the supreme deity among purified deities—having thus understood, weighed, scrutinized, analyzed, and made it manifest—he [spoke].
Regarding the higher divinity through direct knowledge:
the Blessed One knew, understood, touched, and penetrated all things—both superior and inferior—as they relate to the qualities that constitute higher divinity for himself and for others.
What are those qualities that constitute higher divinity for himself?
The right way of practice, the conformable way of practice, the non-contrary way of practice, the way of practice according to the goal, the way of practice in accordance with the Dhamma;
the fulfillment of the precepts, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension,
the four foundations of mindfulness … [as above] … the Noble Eightfold Path.
These are called the qualities that make one’s own self supreme.
What are the qualities that make others supreme?
Right practice … [and so on] … the Noble Eightfold Path.
These are called the qualities that make one a supreme deity among others.
Thus the Blessed One knew, understood, touched, and penetrated the qualities that make one a supreme deity for both himself and others; thus it is said:
"He knew all, both high and low."
"The Teacher who brings an end to questions": the Blessed One is the one who brings an end to, reaches the limit of, defines, and delimits the questions of the *Pārāyaṇa*;

he is the one who brings an end to, reaches the limit of, defines, and delimits the questions of Sabhiya; [he is the one who brings an end to, reaches the limit of, defines, and delimits] the questions of Sakka... and so forth.
of the questions of Suyāma … of the questions of the bhikkhus … of the questions of the bhikkhunīs …
...of the questions of laymen ...
of the questions of laywomen ...
of the questions of kings ...
Of the questions of the khattiyas … of the questions of the brahmins … of the questions of the vessas …
He brings an end to, reaches the limit of, defines the boundaries of,
and establishes the enclosure for questions concerning the pure ones, questions concerning the gods, and questions concerning the Brahmās.
The one who brings an end to questions.
"Teacher" refers to the Blessed One, the caravan leader.
Just as a caravan leader leads a caravan across a wilderness, leads it across a wilderness of robbers, and leads it across a wilderness of wild beasts;
He carries them across a wilderness of famine, he carries them across a wilderness without water—he brings them out, brings them through, and brings them over—bringing them to a land of safety.
In the same way, the Blessed One, the Caravan Leader, carries beings across the wilderness:
he carries them across the wilderness of birth, the wilderness of old age... [and so forth].
He carries them across the wilderness of disease… the wilderness of death… the wilderness of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
He crosses over the wilderness of lust,
the wilderness of hatred,
and the wilderness of delusion.
The wilderness of conceit … the wilderness of views … the wilderness of defilements …
He crosses over the wilderness of misconduct;
he crosses over the thicket of lust; he crosses over the thicket of hatred...
The thicket of delusion … the thicket of views … the thicket of defilements …
He carries them across, brings them out, leads them forth, and causes them to pass over the thicket of misconduct;
he brings them to the security of the deathless Nibbāna—
it is in this sense, too, that the Blessed One is the Caravan Leader.

Alternatively, the Blessed One is a leader, a trainer, one who guides, one who makes things known, one who inspires reflection, one who causes one to see, and one who inspires confidence; thus the Blessed One is a caravan-leader.
Alternatively, the Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path;
he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the skilled master of the path, and his disciples even now follow that path.
“They dwell having attained it afterwards”—thus too the Blessed One is the Caravan-Leader;
the Teacher who brings an end to questions.
“For those who acknowledge their doubts”: those who come with doubts become free from doubt; those who come seeking effacement...
Those who come with blemishes become free from blemishes; those who come with thorns become free from thorns;
those who come with doubt become free from doubt; those who come with lust become free from lust; those who come with hatred become free from hatred;
those who come with delusion become free from delusion; those who come with defilements become free from defilements.
To those who claim to have overcome doubt,
the Elder Piṅgiya said:
"Having directly known the supreme deities..."
He knows all, both high and low;
the Teacher who brings an end to questions for those who confess their doubts.
Unshakable and unassailable,
for which there is no comparison anywhere—
certainly I shall go there; of this I have no doubt.
"Remember me thus as one whose mind is resolute:

unshakable and unagitated. 'Unshakable' refers to the deathless Nibbāna—that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna."
They are unshakable by lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, disparagement, domineering, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud,
obstinacy, impetuosity, pride, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, by all defilements, all misconduct,
all fevers, all taints, all anxieties, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations.
"Nibbāna is unshakeable, permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change"—
this is what is meant by "unshakable. "Unarisen" refers to the deathless Nibbāna, which is said to be unarisen.
That which is the stilling of all formations … the cessation, Nibbāna:
for Nibbāna no arising is discerned, there is no passing away, and no alteration is discerned in it.
Nibbāna is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change.
"Unshakable and unagitated;
for which there is no likeness anywhere.
"For which" refers to Nibbāna.
“There is no simile” means there is no simile, no comparison, no likeness, no counterpart; it does not exist, is not found, and is not obtained.
“Anywhere” means anywhere, in anything, in any place—whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally—of that for which there is no simile anywhere.
"Certainly I shall go; I have no doubt about this.

Here, "certainly" (*addhā*) is a categorical statement, a statement free from uncertainty, a statement free from doubt, a non-duplicative statement, a non-ambiguous statement, a definitive statement, a categorical statement, a non-contradictory statement, and a stabilizing statement—this is what "certainly" means.
"I shall go," "I shall attain," "I shall touch," "I shall realize"—
certainly I shall go.
There is no doubt for me in this regard.
"Herein": there is no doubt regarding Nibbāna, there is no perplexity, there is no wavering, there is no uncertainty;
it does not exist, it is not found, it is not apprehended; it has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
"Truly I shall go; of this I have no doubt.
Bear me in mind thus, with my mind resolutely intent.
"Bear me in mind thus" means: recognize me thus.
"Adhimuttacittaṃ" means: "one whose mind is inclined toward Nibbāna, leaning toward Nibbāna, tending toward Nibbāna, resolved upon Nibbāna"—thus remember me as one whose mind is resolved.
Therefore the Elder Piṅgiya said:
“Unshakable and unassailable,
for whom there is no comparison anywhere—
surely I shall go [to that state]; of this I have no doubt.”
"Thus, remember me as one whose mind is resolute.
This concludes the eighteenth exposition, the verses on the *Pārāyana-anugīti*.
The *Pārāyana-vagga* is complete.
